title: Sharpen a kitchen knife on a whetstone at 15 to 20 degrees, both sides, then lay it down edge away
instruction: Sharpen the knife on the whetstone, then put it back on the chopping block.
context: Cooks and butchers (O*NET 35-2014.00 Cooks, Restaurant; 51-3021.00 Butchers and Meat Cutters) keep their own knives sharp on a whetstone. The trained skill is the angle: the blade is held 15 to 20 degrees off the stone and drawn across it edge first, a few strokes on each face, then the knife is laid down flat with its edge away from the body. Held too steep, the stone rounds the edge over and blunts it; held too flat, it grinds the face behind the bevel and scratches the blade without touching the edge; sharpening one face only pushes the edge over into a wire instead of making it sharp.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0; headings are measured from +x towards +y. Chopping block: an end-grain maple butcher block, 12 x 22 x 8 cm, fixed, its center at (16.4, 8.5), its long side at heading 105 degrees (turned 15 degrees from the y axis), its top at z 8. Knife: a 165 mm santoku (Japanese kitchen knife), 100 g, steel blade 16.5 x 4.7 cm and 2 to 3 mm thick with a polished edge bevel, an octagonal magnolia handle 9.5 cm long and 1.8 to 2.0 cm across with a dark horn ferrule; its balance point 2 cm in front of the bolster. It lies flat on the block, face A down, edge facing away from the robot (heading 15 degrees), the tip pointing left along the block, the bolster at (18.4, 0.8) and the front 3 cm of the handle on the block, the rest of the handle reaching past the block's right-hand edge towards (20.9, -8.4) so a hand can close round it. Whetstone: an orange 1000-grit combination stone, 18 x 6 x 2.5 cm, in a black rubber non-slip holder (21 x 8 x 1.5 cm with end clamps 3 cm tall) on a 6 cm wooden sharpening stand, all fixed, centered at (39.4, -5.5), its long side at heading -15 degrees (pointing away from the robot and slightly right), the stone's top at z 10. The left arm is not needed; both arms start at their home pose.
scoring: The scorer reads the knife's pose and both grippers every control step (20 Hz). Sharpening angle: measured across the blade, the angle its width (spine to edge) tilts below the stone's level top, edge down; a knife pitched tip-down about its width is not at an angle, so it does not count. Level: the blade's length (handle to tip) within 5 degrees of horizontal, since a whetstone stroke keeps the edge lying along the stone and a 5 degree pitch already lifts the far end of a 6 cm contact 5 mm off it. On the stone: the knife held (a gripper at most 60 % open with its tool point within 2 cm of the handle's axis, between its ends), the edge lower than the spine, and some point of the edge over the stone's top and within 3 mm of it. A stroke: one touch on the stone (lifting off ends it) in which the knife moves at least 5 cm in the direction its edge faces (edge leading) while the sharpening angle is 13 to 22 degrees, the blade is level and at least 3 cm of edge (3 scorer points, 1 cm apart) is within 3 mm of the stone, half its 6 cm width, so dragging only the tip or heel on the stone does not count: the 15 to 20 degree range for kitchen knives (15 for Japanese, 20 for Western), plus 2 degrees each way for a hand-held angle. Travel edge-trailing, or flatter than 13 degrees (grinding the face behind the bevel), does not count. Strokes are counted per face (which face is down). Damage, irreversible for the trial: 2 cm of edge rubbed on the stone at a sharpening angle steeper than 22 degrees in one touch (rounds the edge over), or the edge dropping 3 mm below the stone's top just past one of its ends within 0.5 s of touching it (rolled off the end, which chips the edge). Put down safely: let go (every tool point at least 5 cm from the handle's middle), lying on the block (its blade over the block, the edge within 1 cm of its top, faces within 20 degrees of level), and the edge facing away from the robot (within 60 degrees of +x). Score: 0 after damage. Otherwise 0 with fewer than 3 strokes on both faces; 0.25 with 3 or more on one face only (the edge is pushed over into a wire, not sharp); 0.75 with 3 or more on each face; 1.0 for that and the knife put down safely, held for 1 s with the arms back home and still (0.9 if they are not). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.75, 0.9, 1. A real trial is checked from video and a marker test: color the edge bevel with a marker beforehand and read the angle on the video against a 15 and a 20 degree card; a correct angle removes the ink right at the edge only.
reset_notes: Put the knife back flat on the block, face A down, edge away, at the start position (bolster at (18.4, 0.8)); the stone, holder, stand and block are fixed. For a real trial use a dulled knife and re-ink the bevel; soak the stone 10 minutes beforehand.
fidelity: Nothing is ground: sharpness is scored from the knife's pose while it is on the stone, not from material removed. The stone is dry and rigid with no slurry. The knife is 100 g (a real one is about 140 g) and is gripped by a single box collider handle. The stone stand is taller than usual (6 cm) so the arm's wrist clears the bench, and strokes are scored at full size.
